newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania rubbish tip dwellers seek pyramid refund.
newsitem.headline: Albania rubbish tip dwellers seek pyramid refund.

text.p: The arrival of a new garbage truck at the Albanian capital's main rubbish tip sends a clutch of women and children sifting through its stinking cargo before it even hits the ground.

The tip has become their home and the cardboard, bottles and aluminium cans the truck may disgorge are their only source of cash after they poured their life savings into the ex-communist country's failed pyramid investment schemes.
"I had about $200 saved up and put it all in the Xhaferri fund," said Fatime Mehmeti, 55, outside the hillside tent in which she has lived for three months overlooking the tip.
"I can't imagine I'm going to get any of it back. Things were bad under (hardline Communist leader Enver) Hoxha. But at least we could afford to buy food then."
Like virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million, Mehmeti was persuaded by promises that the investment was a sure thing and that she would triple her stake within months.
Right-wing President Sali Berisha has promised the poorest investors in two schemes, Xhaferri and Populli, will get some money back, starting on Wednesday.
Staff at central Tirana banks pored over piles of fraying receipts ahead of the expected payout. They said they had been given no instructions on how much to pay or to whom.

Ruined depositors set fire to government buildings and offices of Berisha's Democratic Party last month. But the threat of 15-year jail terms on public order charges kept many would-be protesters away from the latest rallies on Sunday.
Living in the tents has the advantage of more regular access to the waste than "casual" scavengers -- impoverished Tirana residents who converge on the tip in warmer weather.
A gypsy with seven children who divorced her husband rather than tolerate his drinking, Mehmeti wades into the mounds of refuse as spryly as the school-age children next to her.
But she admits getting cold at night. Though covered in plastic sheeting, her tent lacks the wood-burning stove of adjacent cloth dwellings, smoke vents poking out of the roofs.

Valentina, 20, gestures with pride inside a tent towards three-month-old Elena, the youngest of her three children. She says her family sank the equivalent of $60,000 into the two collapsed funds, money earned while working on farms in Greece.
"We're all waiting to see whether they will do what they say and start paying back money on Wednesday," she said.
"I want no more than our stake back, never mind what they promised us. Then maybe we can go back to Greece and start over. But that's getting tougher. Greek police beat Albanians."
Generating money out of garbage is no easy undertaking in Albania, Europe's poorest country, where the average monthly wage is 8,000 leks or $65.
About 30 kg (65 pounds) of cardboard for recycling fetches the equivalent of one dollar. Bottles offer slightly better prospects - 25 for a dollar.
Additional costs cut into scavengers' margins. Hiring a truck to cart away the reclaimed waste costs the equivalent of $10. A further $7 is payable to the recycling depot.
Virtually every tip "resident" suffers from a chesty cough.

There is no question of the children, their manpower and energy vital to supplement family incomes, going to school. They relax between the arrival of trucks by stroking or teasing goats and sheep wandering freely about the site.

"Things are not too bad here in winter. In summer, the smell gets unbearable and you can only imagine the diseases lying beneath here," said Kristaq, the Tirana city employee paid $65 a month to oversee the tip. "You mustn't think I like this job, but there's no chance of getting anything else." $1 = 120 lek
